title: One Relative Phase Orders Operational Thresholds of Noisy Bell Pairs
abstract: Unlike the two-qubit entangled and CHSH-nonlocal sets, the steerable and Bell-nonlocal ones have no known general closed-form criterion. For any such operational ability whose failing states form a convex set closed under local unitaries, and for a Bell mixture with arbitrary noise, the $X$ part of the noise gives an upper bound on the definitive threshold, the Bell weight above which the mixture attains the ability. That bound is the tightest that the seven of the fifteen Pauli expectation values fixing the $X$ part can support. The same theorem shows that a state has the ability whenever its $X$ part does, so partial tomography of a state can certify its ability. When noise is of $X$ form, the mixture carries a relative phase between the noise and Bell coherences that cannot be gauged away by local unitaries, and it controls the threshold through interference. We prove a monotonicity law: the threshold is nondecreasing in this phase, whether or not a closed-form criterion for the ability exists.
summary: This work develops theoretical tools to precisely determine the operational thresholds for quantum abilities in noisy Bell pairs. It establishes that these thresholds are governed by the relative phase between the noise and coherence terms, proving a general monotonicity law. This provides a powerful, general method for certifying quantum capabilities even when exact analytical criteria are unknown.
main_problem: The paper determines the operational thresholds at which quantum communication abilities (like entanglement or steerability) are lost or regained in noisy Bell pairs.
main_result: It proves a monotonicity law showing that the operational threshold is nondecreasing with the relative phase between the noise and Bell coherences, even when a closed-form criterion is unavailable.
method: The analysis uses the X-part approximation of the noise state and relies on the convexity and local-unitary closure of the ability-absence set to establish bounds and monotonicity theorems.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by noisy Bell pairs represented by a Bell mixture $ho_\lambda(\sigma) = \lambda\Phi_+ + (1 - \lambda)\sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the noise state.
key_observables: Operational thresholds ($\lambda_K$), the relative phase ($	heta$), and the critical radius ($R$) for steerability.
important_parameters: Bell weight ($\lambda$), relative phase ($	heta$), and the seven Pauli expectation values defining the X-part of the noise.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability-absence set $K$ is convex and closed under local unitaries, and it often relies on approximating the noise state by its X-part ($\sigma_X$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the loss/recovery of various quantum abilities along the Bell-mixing line, showing distinct thresholds, and demonstrate that these thresholds are nondecreasing functions of the relative phase $	heta$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the X-part approximation for bounding the threshold, then proving the general monotonicity law concerning the relative phase $	heta$, and finally applying this framework to specific abilities like steerability using geometric constraints.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework developed for analyzing thresholds based on phase dependence and convexity is highly relevant for understanding noise resilience in quantum communication protocols.
